analysis.one_liner: Slows union elections, widens bargaining units, and makes employer workplace rules harder to challenge.
analysis.headline: A bill to slow union elections and shield employer workplace rules went nowhere: it drew zero cosponsors, never left the House Education and Workforce Committee, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act to give employers more time before workers vote on whether to unionize: a hearing could not be held until at least 14 days after a petition is filed, and an election could not be held until at least 20 business days after the National Labor Relations Board orders one [S2][S3]. It would force the Board to bundle most workers into large bargaining units, making a successful vote harder to win, and it would presume most employer handbook rules lawful unless the government proves with clear and convincing evidence that the rule hurts workers more than the employer's justification helps it [S2][S3]. It never advanced beyond committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers with nonunion workforces benefit most. A guaranteed multi-week window before an election gives management time to run an anti-union campaign before employees vote. Requiring all pre-election disputes to be resolved before certification gives employers more opportunities to challenge and delay results. Larger, mixed bargaining units make it harder for small groups of employees to win a vote at all. And presumptively lawful workplace rules would make employer policies that chill organizing very hard to strike down.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the National Labor Relations Board from holding a pre-election hearing until at least 14 calendar days after a union petition is filed, and from holding an election until at least 20 business days after the Board directs one — a guaranteed campaign window for the employer.

Requires the Board to rule on every pre-election issue and challenge before certifying an election result, and lets any party raise issues at any point in the hearing — expanding avenues for employers to contest and delay elections.

Replaces the current standard, under which a proposed unit stands unless excluded workers share an 'overwhelming community of interest,' with a 'sufficient community of interest' test across eight factors — a reversal of the current 'micro-unit' approach that would force larger bargaining units that are harder to organize and win.

Presumes facially neutral employer rules, policies, and handbook provisions lawful, allowing them to be struck down only on clear and convincing evidence that their harm to workers' organizing rights outweighs the employer's justification — and bars the Board from ordering rescission of a rule it deems lawful in a given case.

analysis.who_pays: Employees trying to unionize pay. They would spend more weeks exposed to management pressure before voting, could be diluted into units including many coworkers they don't work alongside, and would face a near-insurmountable evidentiary standard to invalidate employer rules that suppress organizing. The National Labor Relations Board would also bear longer, more complex election processes.

drawbacks.text: Longer pre-election windows expose employees to weeks of employer pressure campaigns — including mandatory meetings — during the exact period when they are deciding whether to unionize; that is precisely why current rules move quickly from petition to election.

Forcing broader bargaining units reverses current law's protection for workers who want to organize with the colleagues they actually work alongside, making a successful union vote substantially harder to achieve.

The bill's stated rationale — that employers deserve time to prepare for a hearing and that elections should be deliberate and well-recorded — is a genuine argument its supporters make; critics respond that the delay itself is the point, because the extended window is when employer pressure happens.

The clear-and-convincing standard and the bar on rescinding lawful rules would leave many neutral-sounding policies — on confidentiality, recording, or outside communications — in place even where they function in practice to discourage organizing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters frame this as fairness for employers: more time to prepare a hearing, clearer rules, and units that reflect how businesses actually operate. But the costs fall on the workers the process is supposed to protect. Delay is the single most effective tool an employer has against an organizing drive, and this bill would guarantee more of it. The combined effect — slower elections, larger units, near-unassailable workplace rules — points in one direction, and the bill's design offers little on the other side of the scale for employees.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and the committee never scheduled a markup or vote — so it simply expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on June 5, 2023.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day, and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, including none from either party.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still sitting in committee, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers seeking to unionize are better off than they would have been under the bill, since current law's shorter election timeline, micro-unit flexibility, and standards for policing employer rules remain in place. Employer groups did not get the delays and rule protections they sought — though they also lost nothing they already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers keep current faster election rules

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.role: House sponsor (R-MI); chairman of the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pushed it as part of a package of employer-favorable National Labor Relations Act amendments, though it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond referral; never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; the only signal is that the Republican sponsor was joined by zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Nonunion employers (retail, logistics, food service, hotels)
industries.note: The bill would hand these employers a guaranteed multi-week window before any union vote, larger and harder-to-win bargaining units, and presumptively lawful workplace rules — the full toolkit for resisting an organizing drive. Ordinary employees on the other side of that toolkit would lose leverage in exactly the same measure.

Slower elections, forced mega-units, and protected employer rules would sharply reduce union win rates. Union fortunes here track directly with workers' ability to exercise their legal right to organize.

industries.industry: Management-side labor law firms and union-avoidance consultants
industries.note: Longer election windows and mandatory rulings on every pre-election issue mean more hearings, litigation, and consulting engagements billed to employers. The workers funding the organizing drive get none of that benefit.
